Mark Zuckerberg was 22 when Yahoo offered $1 billion for Facebook, and his own team wanted him to take it. He went to Steve Jobs instead.

Jobs told him to go to India.

In the video below, Zuckerberg tells India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi what happened next.

"This is a story that I haven't told publicly and very few people know."

Facebook was 2 years old, with about 10 million users. Zuckerberg said no to Yahoo.

It was a tough patch, he says. A lot of people wanted to buy Facebook and thought he should sell.

So he went to one of his mentors, Steve Jobs.

Jobs told him to visit the temple in India he had gone to while figuring out what Apple should be.

Zuckerberg traveled for almost a month. It "reinforced for me the importance of what we were doing."

For early employees with stock, a $1 billion sale is a life-changing payout. Saying no means years of waiting, maybe for nothing.

Within a year of saying no to Yahoo, his entire management team had quit.

He never sold. Today Meta is worth over $1.4 trillion.

Yahoo offered $1 billion.
Steve Jobs offered a temple.

Would you have taken $1 billion at 22, or the ticket to India?

Save the video, and follow for more money stories from behind the world's biggest names.

Deshdrohi Narendra Modi.

Only an Anti-national prime minister will detain and attack people for waving the Indian flag.
Either we are out of ideas or we are cooking. Time will tell

posts.text:
🚨 NEW: Joe Rogan was in shock when historical storyteller Cody Tucker revealed that Mother Teresa was actually a horrible person who kept dying patients in horrible conditions while massive donations flowed to the Vatican:

TUCKER: “She's a scumbag. Mother Teresa never did anything good.”

CONTEXT: In 1994, a physician named Robin Fox visited Mother Teresa's Home for the Dying in Calcutta.

Fox wasn't some anonymous critic.

He was the editor of The Lancet, one of the world's most prestigious medical journals.

And what he described was deeply troubling.

Medical care was inconsistent.

Some decisions were made by nuns and volunteers without formal medical training.

Basic diagnostic investigations were rarely available.

And the facility did not have strong painkillers in its medication supply.

Fox described a patient with a high fever who initially received paracetamol and an antibiotic before a visiting doctor suspected malaria and changed the treatment.

His central objection was that patients who might have treatable conditions weren't being reliably distinguished from people who were actually dying.

Think about that.

Someone could arrive believing they were receiving medical care when they might have needed a proper diagnosis, referral or treatment.

And this wasn't the only criticism.

In 2013, three Canadian academics published a critical review of Mother Teresa's life and work in the journal Studies in Religion.

They questioned her approach to caring for the sick, her political relationships and the management of the enormous donations her organization received.

One of their central concerns was whether a religious belief in the spiritual value of suffering had been allowed to influence the standard of care provided to vulnerable patients.

Mother Teresa believed suffering could have profound spiritual meaning.

But there's a difference between helping someone find meaning in unavoidable suffering...

AND FAILING TO RELIEVE SUFFERING THAT MEDICINE COULD PREVENT.

There is also an important complication.

During the 1990s, India had extraordinarily restrictive regulations governing access to morphine.

Human Rights Watch later documented that India's medical morphine consumption collapsed by approximately 97% between 1985 and 1997.

Even major hospitals struggled to obtain adequate pain medication.

So the absence of strong painkillers at Mother Teresa's facilities does not, by itself, prove she deliberately withheld them because she wanted patients to suffer.

And Fox acknowledged something critics often leave out:

The home he visited provided cleanliness, wound care and genuine kindness to desperately poor people.

The Missionaries of Charity also cared for people whom hospitals had turned away.

Mother Teresa saw her mission primarily as offering dignity, love and spiritual comfort to the abandoned, rather than operating conventional hospitals.

Critics have questioned the Missionaries of Charity's financial transparency for decades.

But Tucker's more specific allegation that Mother Teresa funneled donated money to the Vatican rather than caring for patients has not been established by the evidence reviewed here.

That distinction matters.

IMPORTANT NOTES: Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.

The Catholic Church canonized her as a saint in 2016.

To millions of people, she remains one of the greatest symbols of compassion in modern history.

But the historical record also contains serious criticisms that deserve examination rather than automatic dismissal.

The most disturbing question isn't whether Mother Teresa personally believed suffering had spiritual value.

It's whether that belief, combined with the way her facilities operated, ever resulted in people enduring pain or illness that could have been treated.

Because there is a fundamental difference between helping someone die with dignity...

And allowing someone to suffer when they might not have needed to.

Happy Friyay to you.  Today I am going to tell you about an old fashioned radio show from AR.

Did you know that two boys from Mena, Arkansas, created one of the most popular radio comedy shows in American history?

Chester Lauck and Norris Goff became famous as Lum and Abner when their radio show debuted in 1931. Set in the fictional town of Pine Ridge, Arkansas, the show revolved around two country storekeepers running the Jot 'Em Down Store, where small-town gossip, misunderstandings, and country humor entertained millions of Americans for more than two decades.

But here's where the story gets interesting. The Jot 'Em Down Store was inspired by a real general store in nearby Waters, Arkansas. The radio show became so popular that in 1936, Waters actually changed its name to Pine Ridge in honor of the fictional town.

The original store eventually became part of the Lum and Abner Museum, attracting visitors from across the country. Sadly, the museum closed in 2023 after decades of preserving this wonderful piece of Arkansas history.

But Lum and Abner haven't been forgotten. Mena still celebrates its famous hometown comedians with the annual Lum and Abner Days festival.

Think about that. Two Arkansas boys took everyday small-town life, turned it into a radio show, entertained millions of Americans, and even inspired a town to change its name!
